\subsubsection{The transimpedance loop}

Closing the loop around the electrode changes the stability picture completely. The
amplifier has \SI{88}{\degree} of phase margin; the transimpedance loop built from it
peaks by \SIrange{5.0}{6.4}{\decibel} at about \SI{1}{\kilo\hertz}
(Figure~\ref{fig:tia-zt}), which for a second-order response corresponds to a damping
factor of \numrange{0.25}{0.29} --- a loop closing with \SIrange{25}{30}{\degree} of
margin. Nothing about the amplifier causes this.

The mechanism is the double-layer capacitance at the summing node. The feedback factor
is
\begin{equation}
  \beta(s) = \frac{1}{1 + s R_f C_{\mathrm{dl}}},
\end{equation}
which for $R_f = \SI{560}{\kilo\ohm}$ and $C_{\mathrm{dl}} = \SI{1}{\micro\farad}$ starts
rolling off at \SI{0.28}{\hertz}. The noise gain $1/\beta$ therefore rises at
\SI{20}{\decibel} per decade and meets the amplifier's own \SI{20}{\decibel}-per-decade
roll-off at
\begin{equation}
  f_x = \sqrt{\frac{f_u}{2 \pi R_f C_{\mathrm{dl}}}} \approx \SI{1.3}{\kilo\hertz},
\end{equation}
a \SI{40}{\decibel}-per-decade rate of closure. The measured peak sits at
\SIrange{1.00}{1.12}{\kilo\hertz}, which confirms the mechanism.

The textbook remedy is a feedback capacitor across $R_f$, of value
$C_f = \sqrt{C_{\mathrm{dl}} / (2 \pi R_f f_u)}$. At this gain setting that is of order
\SI{200}{\pico\farad} --- on the order of \SI{0.1}{\milli\metre\squared} of MIM per
channel, and four channels are needed. It is not an on-chip component at this size, and
because $C_f$ scales as $1/\sqrt{R_f}$ the requirement grows, not shrinks, at the lower
gain settings. Resolving this is the principal open item for the stage: the options are
an external capacitor on the WE pad, a deliberate reduction of $f_u$ (the amplifier has
\SI{88}{\degree} of margin to spend), or accepting the peaking and band-limiting after
the ADC. It should be settled before layout, since two of the three change the cell.

DC accuracy, by contrast, is not in question. Transimpedance at \SI{1}{\hertz} is within
\SI{0.02}{\percent} of $R_f$ at every corner, the incremental gain varies by
\SI{0.09}{\percent} across the current range, and the virtual ground holds to
\SI{0.4}{\milli\volt} --- under \SI{0.04}{\percent} of full scale. Below a few hundred
hertz the stage does exactly what it is specified to do.
